headline: Three.js Creator Pairs With AI to Ship Long-Sought Rendering Feature
lede: Ricardo Cabello — known online as @mrdoob — is the creator of Three.js, the JavaScript library that puts GPU-accelerated 3D graphics in browsers. His tweet is brief, but the engineering problem behind it is not: textured RectAreaLights have been on the Three.js community's wish list for years, and he is reporting that a session with Claude moved the needle.
body:
A *RectAreaLight* in Three.js simulates a luminous rectangular surface — think a fluorescent panel, a TV screen, or a window — rather than a point or directional source. It already produces physically plausible soft shadows and gradients, but without texture support it emits a uniform color. Textured area lights take that further: the texture becomes the emission pattern, so a light shaped like a monitor can actually cast the monitor's image into the scene. This is a feature found in production renderers like Arnold and V-Ray but difficult to achieve in real-time WebGL environments.

The difficulty is not conceptual — it is implementation complexity. Area lights require *Linearly Transformed Cosines* (LTC), a mathematical technique that approximates the integral of light arriving from an extended surface without ray-tracing every sample. Layering a texture on top of that approximation requires passing the texture through the same angular transformation, a non-trivial shader change that must interoperate cleanly with Three.js's existing material system, shadow pipeline, and renderer architecture.

The Three.js community forum shows this was a live question as recently as 2024, with developers wanting textured area lights but unclear on when or whether the core library would support them. That @mrdoob himself sat down — with an AI assistant as a collaborator — and shipped it is the meaningful signal here. It suggests that AI pair-programming is useful not just for greenfield feature work by less-experienced developers, but for hard, architecture-aware rendering engineering at the maintainer level of a major open-source project.

For Three.js users, textured RectAreaLights open up richer in-scene advertising panels, realistic interior renders, and real-time lightmap baking workflows that previously required a detour through a separate offline tool. The broader note is that **the gap between what browsers can render and what production tools can render is narrowing**, one shader at a time.

concepts.definition: A light source shaped like a finite rectangle that emits light uniformly across its surface, simulating real-world sources like LED panels or windows. Unlike point lights, it produces soft, spatially varying illumination. In Three.js it is implemented using Linearly Transformed Cosines rather than brute-force sampling.

A mathematical technique for approximating how light from an extended (area) source reflects off a surface in real time. Rather than sampling many rays from the light, LTC transforms the reflection distribution analytically, making area lighting feasible in a GPU rasterizer without path-tracing.

A rendering approach where materials and lights obey real-world energy conservation laws — light that bounces off a surface cannot be brighter than what arrived. PBR became the dominant paradigm in game engines and browser 3D libraries in the 2010s because it produces consistent, predictable results under varied lighting.

An area light source where the emitted light varies spatially according to a texture image, rather than being a uniform color. This lets a panel light cast a projected image — a logo, a gradient, a screen — into the surrounding scene in a physically plausible way.

repos.summary: Three.js is the most widely used JavaScript library for 3D graphics in web browsers, built on WebGL and now also targeting WebGPU. It abstracts shaders, cameras, materials, and scene graphs behind a JavaScript API accessible to web developers without deep graphics expertise. Maintained primarily by Ricardo Cabello (@mrdoob) with thousands of community contributors, it underpins product configurators, games, data visualizations, and creative coding projects across the web.
